JOZINIS WAR ON ELLIES

By: Nicky Troll | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Armed gun men. Dead Elephants. Tourism on Edge. A crime story set in a the world of conservation.

Summary:
More than 20 elephants have been gunned down in recent months in Northern KZN. The
motive goes beyond poaching, it’s believed to be one family’s murderous vendetta.
A local was trampled to death by an elephant in September 2022 – since then at least 20
carcasses have been recovered – some with tusks still in place, some calves, some found
floating in the dam. The pics are gruesome.
This last week, the poachers opened fire on a viewing tour boat with South Africans and
foreign tourists on board.
It’s an all out war up in Pongola, armed gangs poaching on shore and hitting the waters hard
with illegal gill net fishing.
Residents and conservation experts are fearful of the sudden escalation in criminal activity
and senseless killings as the weapons seems to have been turned to people now.


Further information:
STORY IDEA: JOZINI’s WAR ON ELLIES
BACKGROUND
A herd of 74 elephants have been on seven year walkabout originally from the private
Pongola Game Reserve, they’ve wandered into Swaziland via the shallow lake shores, before
returning to South Africa.
The herd ran into conflict with rural communities — culminating in the death of a local
resident in September 2022, who was trampled by an elephant cow.
Some sources have suggested that the death of resident Bheki Nyawo triggered a family
vendetta against the herd, leading to the killing of more than 20 elephants in the area over
recent months. The exact circumstances of that trampling incident remain unclear, but it is
understood that the cow went on the attack in retaliation for the killing of its calf by
elephant poachers.
The conflict has been exacerbated by attempts to control illegal gill-netting of fish in Jozini
Dam by criminal syndicates, along with disputes over cattle grazing in a local nature reserve
close to the Eswatini border.
In one of the most recent incidents, an elephant carcass was discovered floating in the dam
on New Year’s Day with one of its tusks removed.
MOST RECENT INCIDENT – TOURISTS UNDER FIRE
Eight foreign tourists and four South Africans came under gunfire attack on a double-decker
floating tour boat in KwaZulu-Natal on Wednesday.
Shortly after 10.30am on the eastern shores of the Jozini/Pongolapoort dam (on the
southern border between SA and Eswatini) — the occupants of a viewing tour boat dived for

shelter as several shots were fired on their elephant. There is a brief clip of moments
afterwards and the boat trying to get away.
It is understood that there were eight foreign tourists on the boat — five Germans, two
Americans and one Australian — along with four South Africans.
Heinz de Boer, a Democratic Alliance member of the KwaZulu-Natal Legislature and
provincial party spokesman on environmental affairs, has condemned the latest attack on
tourists and elephants and appealed for national intervention.
“Armed groups of poachers have now completely laid siege to the eastern shores of the
lake, with several elephant carcasses recently found, while dozens of gunshots have also
been reported in the region,” he said.
“Guards near the Eswatini border have allegedly also come under attack and infrastructure
damaged and torched by the armed gang.
“The rampant lawlessness and decimation of flora and fauna within this community has long
been highlighted, with the conflict brewing for years. Yet, to date, government has failed to
secure this tourist and wildlife haven.”
Experts remain concerned about the future of the displaced elephant herd, fearing that it
will continue to be slaughtered unless there is urgent intervention.

STRUCTURE: WAR ON ELLIES

VO: Northern KwaZulu Natal. Picturesque Lake Jozini, backed by the Lebombo Mountains. A little slice of paradise with unique biodiversity.

UPSOUND - GUN SHOTS FIRED AS VISUALS TURN TO BLACK AND WHITE – BRING UP IMAGES OF DEAD ELEPHANTS

LINK: This serene environment is now a crime scene with Armed gunmen in hiding. A conservation community on knife's edge and a tourism sector buckling under pressure.

VO: These breath-taking scenes, concealing a dark secret.

In January, a tourist viewing boat was attacked by a group of gun-wielding men on the Eastern Shores of the dam in broad daylight.

Elephant monitor Suzette Boshoff was on the boat that day with international tourists.

SUZETTE: You just hear that panic in the voices. they started screaming. There's people with guns. They're aiming it. US. They aiming it.

VO: Two shots were fired - and then two more.

This clip is of the boat trying to escape the gunmen. The boat beat a desperate retreat; the guests cowering amid the gunshots. They emerged unhurt but traumatised.

UPSOUND VIDEO CLIP?.... Lie down… LIE FLAT…

SUZETTE: They came to Africa for a beautiful African experience and they were actually confronted with the most terrifying moment of their lives. INT5M6

LINK: What has emerged is that the tourists were not the target. They were just inconvenient witnesses. The target of the criminality here, is the environment.

VO: It’s been reported that two elephants were shot that day, three more the next.

This criminality is mainly on the Eastern Bank of the Jozini Lake [along the Lebombo Mountain Range ]- where Mozambique, Swaziland [eswatini] and South Africa meet.

But these were not the first elephants to be killed in the area, and they will not be the last.

This is the inevitable path of a tragedy, years in the making, beginning where nature and humans collide.

NATS AUDIO AS A PAUSE

VO: In September 2022, 46 year old Bheki Nwayo was trampled by an elephant.

NATS AUDIO MOMENT - 1-2 seconds…
As is tradition in Zulu Culture, Bheki is buried alone - because his unnatural death is considered a bad omen.

His father Abnery Nwayo kneels close to his son’s grave and introduces me to his son’s spirit.

UPSOUND “These are the people , they have come to see you and find out what really happened. This is the man. Thank you.

VO: It’s rare for a TV crew to be allowed to visit a grave like this. It's clearly not easy for Nwayo as he's still struggling to come to terms with his son’s sudden death.

NWAYO: My child is dead, what should I do now ?

VO: Looking back, it seems a tragedy was inevitable with the elephants crossing paths with cattle and humans more regularly.

NWAYO: They have been a problem , the problem is that they have calves and they become violent, they don’t want anyone close, that is the problem.

VO: The solution, he says, is simple.

NWAYO: We have been saying these elephants should be removed because this is grazing land and now they are killing us. We are not safe here, we are dying, they elephants are killing us.

VO: Historically the land’s been used by the local community for cattle grazing - but it belongs to Ezemvelo KZN Wildlife and it is a proclaimed protected area.

Joe Phadima is from the organisation’s conservation services, responsible for managing the land that’s in dispute.

JOE: The amount of cattle that were being put there, the livestock. We're not we're not of significant impact or adverse impact to biodiversity.//But that was not to say that it was legal for communities to, you know, to to put animals there.

VO: In other words, the cattle are technically trespassing, but so are the elephants - as they are owned by a private game reserve.

But, this crisis isn't entirely of the elephant's making either. During a drought in 2016, the herd ventured onto the Eastern Shore and became trapped there when the dam levels increased again.

Malcolm Thomson represents an association of private landowners in the Pongola Jozini region.

MALCOLM: It's a very inaccessible area. //despite the fact that we have tried many things over the years with KZN wildlife and tried other efforts to get those animals captured or moved, and unfortunately, that has failed. For various reasons.

VO: With tensions mounting in the community and the elephant's very survival in the balance, stakeholders met in November last year.

Bongani Gumede is a community representative. He was at the meeting and heard first hand the dire warning given by locals. Their intentions were clear.

BONGANI: /the threat was that they will sort the problem out themselves. And soon after that, and towards the end of November, beginning of December, that's when actually the guns started ringing.
MAC: How did you get to a point where, One, A family has lost a child. And two, on the other hand, you've now got people shooting elephants.
BONGANI: communities are not trained in looking after and how to deal with these wild animals. I don't know how legally armed people are, but I can tell you that people do have access to weapons if they need to. //M9 //and they actually can be quite stubborn when they've got a particular viewpoint that they want to defend. Just as they said about the issue of elephants must go.

VO: Since November there have been reports of at least 9 elephants killed. Suzette takes me through the images of their slaughter.

SUZETTE: // that hurts that really hurts me // how do you think this elephant died? It must have been
MAC: this horrific. You can see this is horrible.
SUZETTE: And this is the type of scenes that makes me cry myself to sleep at night. INT3M9

VO: Yet amid the desperation, the authorities were slow to react.

JOE: we asked that they give us a time to look at it. We said we will be engaging together with the private sector, // We request that they exercise patience. //
MAC: But they feel that they have exercised patience for seven years they’ve been speaking about this no body was listening to them //It had to take elephants being shot. It had to take the death of of of Mr. Nwayo’s child for somebody to now stand up and media attention … why should it take media, why should it take death?
JOE: I mean, there is a history of the steps that we've taken, // The problem is that it has not been easy to get permits as there are issues within Swaziland to get permits //We were willing and have always been willing to make sure that we find the means by which we move those adamant elephants as quick as we can.

VO: Again, the elephants became trapped SEVEN years ago - while Ezemvelo is working on it, the herd is being thinned out.

The carcasses are being burnt or covered with rocks to prevent vultures from giving away locations, while the most valuable tusks are being removed in most cases.

BONGANI: When people killed wild animals, they would also take some parts of those animals. So ivory didn't become important now as we know it. It has always been important. // if it was indeed ivory paoching, why would they then kill elephant calves, // without tusks

VO: But others here disagree. What may have started as an act of desperation and self-preservation - is not the only thing at play here.

LINK: //this area has a history of criminality. This is not subsistence hunting. Some believe there is a deeper, more sinister element at work motivated by greed.

MALCOLM: // There's something else happening in that area and the elephant and the cattle are being used as a catalyst to try and drive whatever they're trying to achieve on that side.

VO: It’s not just elephants being hunted - hippos and crocodiles are taken out too. There’s also large scale illegal gill net fishing and rhino poaching. The eastern shore has become a free-for-all.

Barend Lottering is an anti-poaching security expert.

BAREND: // anything that's got the slightest value for money would be would be taken out. It's organized crime. You know, it's cross-border crime and there's huge amounts of money to be made.
MAC: HAS Changed over time as it evolved and has become more serious over time.
BAREND: // NOW. THERE’S MORE VIOLENCE INVOVLEd, THERE’S MORE FIREARMS INVOLVED. THE GROUPS ARE BIGGER. // a couple of months ago, // A policeman was shot in the face, shot with a high caliber weapon.

VO: While the policeman survived the attack, and is still undergoing reconstructive surgery - it’s clear the syndicates behind the criminality will not let anyone get in the way - intimidation is rife and even informants are fearful.

BAREND: // they also know that their lives are worth nothing if it comes out that they've been giving information. // These gangs look after each other //

VO: Private landowners invest hundreds of millions of rands in land, infrastructure and employment, but bear the brunt of criminality.

MALCOLM: //we have experienced a number of cancellations already // And people are now starting to wonder whether it's safe to come to visit our reserves. M5

VO: The private landowners have security teams patrolling their land, the criminality is entirely limited to the notorious east bank.

BAREND BOAT: / And the bottom part of the mountain, the smuggling routes. the mountain is where the three countries come together. And Mozambique, South Africa and Swaziland.
MAC: Yeah.
BAREND BOAT: And so if they commit the crime. Yeah. And law enforcement is onto them, they can either decide to go across into Mozambique or they can go to Swaziland.

VO: Finding a solution has never been more urgent, as criminal elements appear to take advantage of conflict on the Eastern Shores.

SUZETTE: //It's spreading like wildfire. And especially after you've been hunting the top species, you've been shooting on tourists. And you still scot free. // this whole area currently, I believe, is under threat. If we don't react and start governing and protect these areas.

VO: Ezemvelo needs to take the lead - it’s Ezemvelo’s land and it’s their duty.

MAC: When we speak to the community within that northern KwaZulu-Natal area, fingers pointed at you. //
JOE: Ezemvelo has been blamed, because Ezemvelo is responsible for biodiversity // taking responsibility over that is not making miracles. You know, we we work within in a constrained space. // to make sure that we resolve their issues and do as best as we can to do that. And sometimes that falls short.

VO: The new plan is to move the elephants during the winter months and increase police patrols, but time is running out.

MALCOLM: // If this had to be lost to conservation and to ecotourism, // it would be a very sad day, not just for KZN and our community, but for South Africa as a whole.

VO: But for some the loss is much more personal. As we finished our interview, Nwayo kneels again at his son’s grave.

NWAYO: It is ok, [pause] They are leaving now [pause] Rest well.


[END]

Is it just a clash between humans and wildlife or is it a criminal network at play.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Armed gun men. Dead Elephants. Tourism on Edge. A crime story set in a the world of conservation.
metadata.Summary: More than 20 elephants have been gunned down in recent months in Northern KZN. The motive goes beyond poaching, it’s believed to be one family’s murderous vendetta. A local was trampled to death by an elephant in September 2022 – since then at least 20 carcasses have been recovered – some with tusks still in place, some calves, some found floating in the dam. The pics are gruesome. This last week, the poachers opened fire on a viewing tour boat with South Africans and foreign tourists on board. It’s an all out war up in Pongola, armed gangs poaching on shore and hitting the waters hard with illegal gill net fishing. Residents and conservation experts are fearful of the sudden escalation in criminal activity and senseless killings as the weapons seems to have been turned to people now.
metadata.Further information: STORY IDEA: JOZINI’s WAR ON ELLIES BACKGROUND A herd of 74 elephants have been on seven year walkabout originally from the private Pongola Game Reserve, they’ve wandered into Swaziland via the shallow lake shores, before returning to South Africa. The herd ran into conflict with rural communities — culminating in the death of a local resident in September 2022, who was trampled by an elephant cow. Some sources have suggested that the death of resident Bheki Nyawo triggered a family vendetta against the herd, leading to the killing of more than 20 elephants in the area over recent months. The exact circumstances of that trampling incident remain unclear, but it is understood that the cow went on the attack in retaliation for the killing of its calf by elephant poachers. The conflict has been exacerbated by attempts to control illegal gill-netting of fish in Jozini Dam by criminal syndicates, along with disputes over cattle grazing in a local nature reserve close to the Eswatini border. In one of the most recent incidents, an elephant carcass was discovered floating in the dam on New Year’s Day with one of its tusks removed. MOST RECENT INCIDENT – TOURISTS UNDER FIRE Eight foreign tourists and four South Africans came under gunfire attack on a double-decker floating tour boat in KwaZulu-Natal on Wednesday. Shortly after 10.30am on the eastern shores of the Jozini/Pongolapoort dam (on the southern border between SA and Eswatini) — the occupants of a viewing tour boat dived for shelter as several shots were fired on their elephant. There is a brief clip of moments afterwards and the boat trying to get away. It is understood that there were eight foreign tourists on the boat — five Germans, two Americans and one Australian — along with four South Africans. Heinz de Boer, a Democratic Alliance member of the KwaZulu-Natal Legislature and provincial party spokesman on environmental affairs, has condemned the latest attack on tourists and elephants and appealed for national intervention. “Armed groups of poachers have now completely laid siege to the eastern shores of the lake, with several elephant carcasses recently found, while dozens of gunshots have also been reported in the region,” he said. “Guards near the Eswatini border have allegedly also come under attack and infrastructure damaged and torched by the armed gang. “The rampant lawlessness and decimation of flora and fauna within this community has long been highlighted, with the conflict brewing for years. Yet, to date, government has failed to secure this tourist and wildlife haven.” Experts remain concerned about the future of the displaced elephant herd, fearing that it will continue to be slaughtered unless there is urgent intervention.
